# opencode-session-finder

An [OpenCode](https://opencode.ai) plugin that searches the text of previous sessions. It adds
a **Search sessions** command to OpenCode Desktop and the terminal interface. The agent can also
search with `search_sessions` and switch terminal sessions with `open_session`.

The OpenCode session list matches titles only. This plugin reads the messages of every session
in the local database.

Requires OpenCode 2.3 or later.

## Search from OpenCode Desktop

1. Choose **Search sessions** from the command palette or enter `/search-session` in the composer.
2. Enter a keyword or sentence and select **Search**. To search immediately, enter
   `/search-session <keyword or sentence>`.
3. Select a result's title to open the session in a tab.

Title matches appear first, followed by message matches. Results show the last match date and an
excerpt. The search excludes the current session on the desktop app's own server and shows up to
30 sessions. When viewing a remote session, the command still searches the desktop app's own
server, not the remote server.

OpenCode Web doesn't load third-party GUI plugins. To search from Web, ask the agent to use
`search_sessions` on a server where the plugin is installed.

## Search from the terminal

Open the search with **`<leader>f`** (**Ctrl+X**, then **F**), from the command palette
(**Ctrl+P**) as **Search sessions**, or with `/search-session <keyword or sentence>`.

- Without arguments, the command asks for a keyword or sentence. A search takes several
  seconds on a large database, longer when it falls back to tool output.
- The results list opens right away and fills in as the search runs. Sessions whose titles
  match, such as an MR ID in the title, appear first, within a fraction of a second. The other
  matches appear below them when the message search finishes, without moving the selection.
  The list title shows the search's progress, and closing the list cancels the search.
- Within the title matches and within the other matches, sessions of the current project come
  first. Each entry shows its project, the date of its last match and an excerpt, plus the
  directory for sessions of other projects. The title notes when the results come from a
  fallback search.
- The list's filter keeps sessions whose title or project contains each typed word, in their
  existing order.
- **Enter** focuses the session's tab, or switches to it for child sessions or when tabs are
  off. Sessions of other projects stay closed, and a toast shows the
  `opencode --session <id>` command to reopen them.
- **Ctrl+S** (**Summarize here**) queues a prompt in the current session that asks the agent to
  read the session's matches with `search_sessions` and summarize them.
- When nothing matches, the list title lists the searches that ran.

The search excludes the session on screen and shows at most 30 sessions.

## Search with the agent

Ask the agent which earlier session discussed something. It calls `search_sessions`, presents
the matches, and offers to open one, summarize it, or show more matches.

`search_sessions` accepts these options besides `query`:

| Option                         | Effect                                                                                            |
| ------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `words`                        | Matches sessions that contain every word, in any message.                                         |
| `include`                      | Also searches `tools` (commands, file reads, and tool output), `reasoning`, or `system` messages. |
| `fallback`                     | Set to `false` to run only the requested search.                                                  |
| `session_id`                   | Searches one session, for example to read more of its matches.                                    |
| `directory`                    | Searches sessions in a directory and its subdirectories.                                          |
| `current_project`              | Searches sessions of the current project, including its other worktrees.                          |
| `since`, `until`               | Limits matches to a date range (`YYYY-MM-DD`). `until` excludes that day.                         |
| `limit`, `excerpts`, `context` | Sets the number of sessions (10), excerpts per session (3), and characters around a match (100).  |
| `include_current`              | Also searches the calling session.                                                                |

User messages, assistant replies, compaction summaries, and titles are always searched.
Matching is literal and case-insensitive. When a search finds nothing, it's retried with
`words` for a multi-word query, then with tool output included.

`open_session` focuses another session of the current project in the terminal that shows the
calling session. Pass `close_source: true` to close the calling session's tab afterward. Closing
a tab keeps the conversation in history. The tool fails for sessions of other projects, and
after 3 seconds when no terminal shows the calling session.

## How it works

The server plugin reads the OpenCode database read-only with `bun:sqlite`, in a worker thread
so a long search doesn't block other sessions. The terminal interface asks the server to run
its searches, so a terminal attached to a remote server searches that server's sessions.

The server can't drive the terminal, so `open_session` sends an event that the terminal
interface handles. Only the terminal that shows the calling session, or one of its ancestors,
acts on it.

A session is part of the current project when it has the same project ID. Directories outside a
repository share the `global` project, so those sessions must also share a directory. Without a
current session, such as on the home screen, the project comes from the directory.

The search depends on OpenCode's internal database schema: the `session_message` table and
`session_v2`, or `session` on older versions. ASCII letters match in any case; other letters
must match the case of the query.

## Installation

```bash
opencode plugin add opencode-session-finder
```

This adds the plugin to `~/.config/opencode/opencode.json`. OpenCode loads the Desktop and
terminal interfaces from the same package:

```json
{
  "plugins": ["opencode-session-finder"]
}
```

## Options

| Option     | Default                                                 | Description                              |
| ---------- | ------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------- |
| `database` | `${XDG_DATA_HOME:-~/.local/share}/opencode/opencode.db` | Path of the OpenCode database to search. |

```json
{
  "plugins": [
    { "package": "opencode-session-finder", "options": { "database": "/path/to/opencode.db" } }
  ]
}
```

The terminal interface takes its options from `cli.json`. Add the plugin there with the same
package name or path as in `opencode.json`:

| Option       | Default | Description                                                                 |
| ------------ | ------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `animations` | `true`  | Animates the results list title while searching. `false` shows `⋯` instead. |

```json
{
  "plugins": [{ "package": "opencode-session-finder", "options": { "animations": false } }]
}
```

# opencode-terminal-progress

An [OpenCode](https://opencode.ai) CLI plugin that shows agent progress in your terminal tab using
[OSC 9;4](https://iterm2.com/documentation-escape-codes.html) progress reporting.

Requires OpenCode 2. For OpenCode 1, install the `opencode-v1` dist-tag
(`npm install opencode-terminal-progress@opencode-v1`).

## Supported terminals

| Terminal                                                  | Detection                                                   |
| --------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- |
| [Ghostty](https://ghostty.org)                            | `TERM_PROGRAM=ghostty`                                      |
| [iTerm2](https://iterm2.com)                              | `TERM_PROGRAM=iTerm.app`, `LC_TERMINAL`, `ITERM_SESSION_ID` |
| [kitty](https://sw.kovidgoyal.net/kitty/)                 | `KITTY_WINDOW_ID`, `TERM_PROGRAM=kitty`                     |
| [WezTerm](https://wezfurlong.org/wezterm/)                | `TERM_PROGRAM=WezTerm`, `WEZTERM_EXECUTABLE`                |
| [Windows Terminal](https://github.com/microsoft/terminal) | `WT_SESSION`                                                |

The plugin automatically detects which terminal is in use and becomes a no-op if none of the above
are found. tmux passthrough is handled transparently when `$TMUX` is set.

kitty is supported on **0.47+**: kitty draws an in-window progress bar since 0.47 (see the
`progress_bar` option in `kitty.conf`), while 0.39-0.46 only showed a percentage in the tab title
and earlier versions treated OSC 9;4 as notifications. kitty does not set `TERM_PROGRAM`, so it is
detected via `KITTY_WINDOW_ID` (also inside tmux), unless another terminal nested in kitty has set
`TERM_PROGRAM`. The plugin stays inactive unless it can confirm the version is at least 0.47 by
running `kitty --version` on the running emulator (`/proc/<KITTY_PID>/exe`, Linux) or on the binary
in `KITTY_INSTALLATION_DIR` (Linux and macOS).

Set `OPENCODE_TERMINAL_PROGRESS=0` (or `false`/`no`) to disable progress reporting.

## Progress states

| Agent state       | Progress indicator |
| ----------------- | ------------------ |
| Busy              | Indeterminate      |
| Idle              | Cleared            |
| Error             | Error (red)        |
| Waiting for input | Paused at 50%      |

# opencode-tmux-indicator

An [OpenCode](https://opencode.ai) CLI plugin that sets a tmux window option
(`@opencode-waiting`) when the agent is waiting for user input (permission prompt or question),
and clears it when the agent resumes.

Requires OpenCode 2. For OpenCode 1, install the `opencode-v1` dist-tag
(`npm install opencode-tmux-indicator@opencode-v1`).

## How it works

Tracks waiting conversations separately and sets `@opencode-waiting 1` on their tmux window.
The flag stays set until every plugin instance in the window has cleared its waiting sessions.
A 3-second startup grace period delays indicators, preserving requests that remain pending.

The plugin also writes a BEL character to the pane TTY so tmux sets the
`window_bell_flag` on the window. This lets you jump to the next waiting window
with `Prefix + M-n` (`next-window -a`).

You can use the option in your tmux status line to show a visual indicator, e.g.:

```
set -g status-right "#{?@opencode-waiting, waiting,} #H"
```

The plugin is a no-op when `$TMUX` or `$TMUX_PANE` are not set.

## Navigate to a waiting conversation

Each plugin instance publishes a pane option named `@opencode-waiting-target-<instance ID>`.
Its value is an HTTP Unix socket path inside a private temporary directory. Use
`tmux show-options -p -t PANE` to discover the options, then read each value with
`tmux show-option -pqv -t PANE OPTION`.

The socket accepts two requests:

- `GET /waiting` returns a sorted JSON array of currently waiting OpenCode session IDs.
- `POST /select/SESSION_ID` displays a waiting session in the OpenCode terminal interface that
  owns the socket. It returns `true` once the plugin has asked the interface to show the session,
  HTTP 404 if the session is no longer waiting, or HTTP 502 if navigation fails.

The plugin runs inside the terminal interface, so it focuses the session's tab when session tabs
are enabled and otherwise navigates to the session. OpenCode does not need to expose a TCP port.

Navigators should query each socket, cycle through individual sessions, and remove stale pane
options when the owning process has exited.

## Install a local build

Run `mise run install-local tmux-indicator` from the repository root to install a bundled copy
at `~/.config/opencode/plugins/tmux-indicator/tui.js`. Remove the npm plugin entry from your
`cli.json` to avoid loading both copies, then restart OpenCode.

## Recommended tmux settings

The BEL trigger works with tmux's default `monitor-bell on` setting. To prevent
the bell from forwarding to your terminal emulator (which may play a sound or
flash), add these to your `tmux.conf`:

```tmux
set -gw window-status-bell-style default  # prevent the bell style from overriding your custom status format
set -g bell-action none                   # suppress BEL forwarding and messages; window_bell_flag is still set
```

## Prerequisites

[tmux](https://github.com/tmux/tmux) must be running and `$TMUX` / `$TMUX_PANE` set in the
environment where OpenCode is launched.

## Installation

```bash
opencode plugin add opencode-tmux-indicator
```

This adds the plugin to `~/.config/opencode/cli.json`:

```json
{
  "plugins": ["opencode-tmux-indicator"]
}
```

The plugin runs in the terminal interface, which is where `$TMUX` and `$TMUX_PANE` are set, so it
keeps working when the CLI connects to a remote server.

# Forgekeeper reference

For installation and everyday use, see the [Forgekeeper README](../README.md).

An [OpenCode](https://opencode.ai) plugin that tracks the issues or PRs/MRs a session works on.
It prefixes the session title with their references, shows the PR/MR status in the prompt
footer, and surfaces new review feedback in a persistent inbox. It supports GitLab and GitHub. The status
and review notifications are optional; see [Keep only session titles](#keep-only-session-titles).

![OpenCode session environment with issue and MR references, a review notification, and a footer tracking four merge requests.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/pedropombeiro/opencode-plugins/main/packages/forgekeeper/images/session-review-notification.png)

Notification wording has changed since this capture.

Requires OpenCode 2.2 or later. It replaces
[`opencode-forge-session-title`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/opencode-forge-session-title); see
[Migrating from opencode-forge-session-title](#migrating-from-opencode-forge-session-title).

## Installation

```bash
opencode plugin add opencode-forgekeeper
```

This adds the plugin to your `opencode.json`:

```json
{
  "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
  "plugins": ["opencode-forgekeeper"]
}
```

The package has a server entry point and a CLI entry point, which OpenCode loads automatically.
The server owns session targets, title prefixes, forge lookups, polling, and notification
delivery. The CLI holds leases on the sessions it has shown, their latest snapshots, and each
directory's settings. It renders the status that the server serves and shows its notices as
toasts.

### Requirements

- [`glab`](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/cli) for GitLab and [`gh`](https://cli.github.com/)
  for GitHub, on the `PATH` of the OpenCode server. Each is only needed for its forge.
- Each CLI logged in to every host it's used for: `glab auth login --hostname <host>` and
  `gh auth login --hostname <host>`. The plugin uses their credentials and has none of its
  own.
- For self-managed GitLab hosts not named `gitlab.*`, and for GitHub Enterprise, the
  `hosts` and `githubHosts` [options](#options).

Without a forge CLI, titles still follow targets and branches, and `/forge-status` reports
what's missing, such as `glab is not installed`.

## Upgrade from forgekeeper 2.x

Forgekeeper 3 changes where review notifications go, and renames its options:

- **Notifications:** review feedback goes to the `/forge-feedback` inbox and starts a
  restricted summary turn when configured, without asking the agent to address it. Set
  `delivery.reviews` to `"inbox"` to stop automatic session delivery, or `"passive"` to queue
  a notice without starting a turn. See
  [Review notifications](#review-notifications).
- **Options:** Forgekeeper no longer reads the former option names. It shows an error toast
  that names each one, and uses that option's default instead. For example, a former
  `reviewStatus: false` leaves status on, so rename it to `status: false` before you upgrade.
- **Monitoring:** Forgekeeper also watches recent sessions with PR/MR targets that no CLI
  has shown, and announces conflicts, failed jobs, and merges of their targets. See
  [Which sessions the server watches](#which-sessions-the-server-watches) and
  [Merge request updates](#merge-request-updates). Set `watch.lifecycle` to `false` to
  stop the merge request updates.

Rename the former options as follows:

| Former option                               | Now                                                                                     |
| ------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `reviewStatus`                              | `status`                                                                                |
| `notifyHumanReviews`                        | `watch.humanReviews`                                                                    |
| `notifyAutomatedReviews`, `notifyDuoReview` | `watch.automatedReviews`, and `watch.reviewBots` for review bots                        |
| `resumeSession`                             | `delivery.reviews`: `"summary"` starts a turn, and `"passive"` queues for the next turn |

## Session targets

The server registers the `set_session_target` tool and adds instructions to the agent's
context. The current target is stored in the `forgekeeper-session-target` session instruction
entry. Updates take effect at the next step without changing the system prompt.
When you establish or change the primary issue, PR, or MR, the agent sets its full
URL as the session target. Background references, comparisons, and dependencies keep the
current target. Reviewing, triaging, or addressing feedback on existing issues and PRs/MRs
also sets them as targets, including ones a skill or search found rather than ones you linked.
After the agent creates a PR/MR for the current task, it sets the new PR/MR
as the target, passing the current issue as `issue_url`.

For example, if the title starts with `[#123, !45]` and you ask the agent to review MR `!456`,
the prefix becomes `[!456]`. Without `issue_url`, the server reads the PR/MR's source branch
and takes the issue number from its name, so reviewing an MR from `321-fix-timeout` produces
`[#321, !456]`.

Targets persist per session across plugin reloads. A forked session starts with the targets of
the session it was forked from, as they are when Forgekeeper first updates the fork, and keeps
them from then on. Calling `set_session_target` with
`target: "branch"` returns to branch-based naming. Child sessions and untitled sessions are
skipped.

### Several targets

A session can work on up to 50 issues and PRs/MRs at once, such as a set of related MRs
under review. Pass their full URLs in `targets` instead of `target`, and choose how they
change the current targets with `operation`:

| `operation`         | Effect                                                                         |
| ------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `replace` (default) | Sets exactly the given targets.                                                |
| `add`               | Appends the given targets and keeps the current ones.                          |
| `remove`            | Drops the given targets. Removing the last one returns to branch-based naming. |

```json
{
  "targets": [
    "https://gitlab.com/group/project/-/merge_requests/101",
    "https://gitlab.com/group/other/-/merge_requests/102"
  ],
  "operation": "add"
}
```

The server normalizes and deduplicates the URLs, which can come from different projects.

With `targets`, `issue_url` relates every listed target to the same issue, such as a set of
MRs for one issue. Every target must then be a PR/MR from the issue's forge. With
`operation: "add"`, only the added targets get the issue.

The agent guidance is generic. When you ask the agent to work on several issues or PRs/MRs,
it sets all of them as targets. If you describe them instead of linking them, the agent
finds them first, then sets them. After it creates a PR/MR for a task with several targets,
it adds the new one instead of replacing the others.

With several targets, the title prefix lists their own references, such as `[!101, !102]`.
When every target has the same related issue, from `issue_url` or from its source branch
name, the issue comes first, such as `[#12, !101, !102]`. More than four targets list the
first three and count the rest, such as `[!101, !102, !103, +3]`.

Target URLs can name a GitLab MR, issue, or work item on any host, or a GitHub PR or issue.
GitHub URLs are accepted on any host that isn't recognizably GitLab, so GitHub Enterprise
targets work.

## Branch-based naming

Without an explicit target, the title follows the checked-out branch:

1. The prefix starts with the issue number from the branch name, or the branch name
   without one.
2. It adds the newest open PR/MR from the branch, or `!N/A` (GitLab) or `#N/A` (GitHub)
   until one exists.

The title is reconciled after target changes, title changes, and successful agent runs.
Text you add to the title, including your own bracketed prefixes, is kept.

Branch names longer than 40 characters are shortened with an ellipsis in the prefix. Titles
stay within 100 characters by shortening the text after the prefix, never the prefix
itself, so the plugin can still find and replace its prefix later.

The default branch and branches named `main`, `master`, `develop`, or `HEAD` get no prefix.

The branch's remote, pushed branch name, and forge come from the same repository discovery
as the status footer. That discovery uses the branch's push or upstream remote, recognizes
forks, and classifies hosts with the `hosts` and `githubHosts` options.

| Pattern                           | Example branch          | Issue |
| --------------------------------- | ----------------------- | ----- |
| `<prefix>/<number>-<description>` | `feature/123-add-login` | `123` |
| `<number>-<description>`          | `123-fix-typo`          | `123` |
| `<description>-<number>`          | `fix-typo-123`          | `123` |
| `<prefix>/<number>/<description>` | `user/123/some-work`    | `123` |
| `issue-<number>`, `gh-<number>`   | `gh-42-improve-perf`    | `42`  |
| `fix-<number>`, `feat-<number>`   | `fix-99`                | `99`  |

## Status footer

The server picks each session's PRs/MRs in this order:

1. The explicit targets.
1. A PR/MR number in a title prefix that you wrote, such as `!456` in `[!456] Review`.
1. The checked-out branch's open PRs/MRs.

A prefix that the plugin wrote from the branch doesn't count as a title reference, so the
footer follows the branch when its PR/MR closes and another opens. The title prefix itself
reuses a branch's PR/MR number for up to 10 minutes.

Explicit targets that aren't PRs/MRs, such as issues, show no status. Unresolved explicit
PRs/MRs never fall back to the branch.

Without a PR/MR to show, the footer stays empty, even when a lookup fails, such as in a new
session before the server answers. It shows `PR/MR status unavailable` only when none of
the session's explicit PR/MR targets can be looked up or found. `/forge-status` explains
why.

The server runs at most four `glab` or `gh` commands at once for status and review
feedback, across all sessions. When some target lookups fail, the footer shows the others
and counts the failures as `N unavailable`. A target whose lookup failed with an error
keeps its previous status until a later poll succeeds. A GitLab response that reports an
error counts as a failed lookup, never as a missing MR, so it's retried with backoff.

When the CLI can't reach the server, such as while the server plugin reloads, the footer
keeps the last status and marks it `stale`. The CLI never looks PRs/MRs up itself, so it
can't show another project's PR/MR with the same number as a target.

With several PR/MR targets, the footer shows counts instead of one PR/MR's status, such as
`5 MRs · 🤖 2 reviewing · 1 CI failed · 1 conflict · 1 merged`. Clicking it opens the
status dialog, which lists each PR/MR.

![Compact Forgekeeper footer tracking four MRs, with one conflict and two merged.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/pedropombeiro/opencode-plugins/main/packages/forgekeeper/images/conflict-status-footer.png)

The footer shows checks or the pipeline, unresolved threads, conflicts, approval, and a
running automated review, from GitLab Duo or GitHub Copilot. GitHub also shows a requested
change. Unknown mergeability stays unknown rather than appearing conflict-free.

The status dialog separates pipeline results, unresolved threads, and review requirements:

![Forgekeeper status dialog showing a passed pipeline, one unresolved thread, no conflicts, and approval requirements not yet satisfied despite a GitLab Duo approval.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/pedropombeiro/opencode-plugins/main/packages/forgekeeper/images/review-and-ci-status.png)

The footer shows `approved` only when GitLab reports that approval requirements are met,
at least one person approved, and every human reviewer approved. Bot approvals, such as
Duo's, don't count. While human reviewers haven't approved, it shows `awaiting @username`,
or `awaiting N reviewers` for more than two.

Clicking the PR/MR number or pipeline opens it in the browser. Clicking any other indicator
opens the status dialog. These commands are also available from the command palette:

- `/forge-status` opens a dialog with full status and a refresh action. Aliases:
  `/mr-status` and `/pr-status`.
- `/forge-open` opens the PR/MR in the browser. Aliases: `/mr-open` and `/pr-open`.

### Desktop app

OpenCode Desktop loads Forgekeeper's desktop part, so it matches the terminal UI:

- A pill above the composer shows the footer's indicators and the session's update count.
  Its menu opens the PR/MR and pipeline links, the status panel, and the inbox panel.
- `/forge-status` opens a side panel with the status dialog's details and a refresh action.
- `/forge-feedback` opens a side panel with the checkout's updates. Each update offers its
  links and **Open session**, **Summarize in session**, **Act on feedback**, **Retry**, and
  **Acknowledge**, and the panel can pause or resume monitoring.
- `/forge-open` opens the PR/MR in the browser, or asks which one to open.
- Server notices appear as toasts, and as system notifications when no app window has
  focus, following **Settings > Notifications**.

The desktop part watches only sessions on the app's own server. It uses OpenCode's
experimental GUI plugin API, which may change between releases. Settings > Extensions >
Plugins can turn it off without affecting the server part.

### Web app

The OpenCode web app runs no terminal or desktop plugin parts, so it has no footer, panels,
toasts, or `/forge-status`, `/forge-open`, and `/forge-feedback`. Monitoring doesn't depend
on them: the server watches [discovered sessions](#which-sessions-the-server-watches)
without a client. To see updates in the web app, set `delivery.reviews` and
`delivery.lifecycle` to `summary`. A `passive` notice is queued until the session's next
turn, and the web app shows only its title.

The server registers two commands that every client offers, while status is on, including
the web app:

- `/forge-report` refreshes the session's status and shows what `/forge-status` shows.
- `/forge-inbox` lists the session's pending updates, newest first, with their stable IDs and
  links. `/forge-inbox ack <id>` and `/forge-inbox ack all` acknowledge updates, and
  `/forge-inbox summarize <id>` starts the update's summary turn, as Ctrl+R does in
  `/forge-feedback`. Use the displayed ID rather than the update's position.

The apps don't display the text of a synthetic message, so each answer runs as a
tool-free turn in which the session's model shows Forgekeeper's report. The report is
written from forge data, such as titles and branch names, which the request marks as data.
Like a [summary turn](#summary-turns), only the turn's request holds the report, and its
record stays in plugin storage until the next user prompt or for at most 7 days. The
commands take other names than the CLI's, so the terminal UI doesn't list them twice.

Reports use an output budget based on their size, separate from the summary limit. Reports
larger than 6,000 UTF-8 bytes end at a complete line and include a notice that content was
omitted. Open the Desktop or terminal panels to read the complete report.

The server caches each session's status and polls every 2 minutes while a CLI shows an open
PR/MR, or every 30 seconds while an automated review runs or new review feedback waits for
its quiet period. Each change reaches the CLIs as
an RPC event.

Sessions in the same checkout share cached status and human-feedback fetches for the same
forge, host, project, and PR/MR number. Overlapping requests share one in-flight fetch.
Successful status results remain fresh for the polling interval, capped at 30 seconds
while an automated review runs. Complete human-feedback results remain fresh for 60 seconds.
Failures and incomplete feedback are not retained for reuse. Each cache keeps at most
1,000 entries and is cleared when

## Merge request updates

Forgekeeper also watches each session's explicit PR/MR targets for three changes:

- **Conflicts:** a target that could merge starts to conflict with its target branch.
- **Failed jobs:** a job fails in a target's head pipeline, even while the pipeline still
  runs.
- **Merges:** a target merges.

All come from the forge's own state, compared between two lookups, never from comments
such as GitLab's "can no longer be merged" note. The first lookup of a target only records
it, so nothing that happened before Forgekeeper first saw the target is announced. Records
persist across restarts, so a change that happened while OpenCode wasn't running is
announced at the next lookup. A
mergeability the forge hasn't settled yet, such as while GitLab rechecks an MR after a
push to it or to its target branch, keeps the last known state. A conflict that ends and
starts again is a new update.
Sessions are watched the same way as for review feedback, without visiting their tabs.

Failed jobs don't wait for the pipeline to finish, which can take much longer than the
job. Each lookup reads the pipeline's failed jobs:

- On GitLab, the first 10 failed jobs that aren't retried, with the MR, and no other
  query. One that isn't allowed to fail is enough to know the pipeline fails. When all
  10 are allowed to fail and more failed, an unread one may fail the pipeline, but none
  counts as failing it while the pipeline runs. Once the pipeline finishes as failed,
  which jobs allowed to fail never cause, the update reports that a job past those 10
  failed it.
- On GitHub, the head commit's failed checks, which count as one pipeline.

Each job attempt counts once. A lookup that finds new failed jobs makes one update for
them, which names and links them, lists the jobs that failed earlier in that pipeline,
and says whether the pipeline still runs. That update replaces the pipeline's earlier one
in the inbox, and reaches the session again. A retry that fails again is a new attempt,
so it's a new failure. Forgekeeper remembers the newest 500 attempts it saw in a pipeline,
so one that newer failures push past the jobs it reads isn't new when it comes back.
Another pipeline that fails, such as after a push, is new too. At
most 10 jobs are named, and more are counted. Records stored before Forgekeeper told job
attempts apart only record the jobs, without an update. The update clears once the
pipeline no longer has failed jobs, another pipeline replaces it, or the PR/MR closes.
Forgekeeper never retries or fixes failed jobs. A rule can have it
[investigate them](#investigate-failed-jobs) in the owning session.

Each change waits in the target's record until it reaches the inbox, in the same storage
write as the record. A merge stops polling, so waiting changes are retried every minute
and after a reload, without another lookup. Updates go to `/forge-feedback`, and
`delivery.lifecycle` sets what else they do: `"inbox"`, the default, `"passive"`, or
`"summary"`, as for [review feedback](#review-notifications). Each change keeps the mode
from when it was detected, so turning on summaries never starts turns for changes found
earlier. A summary turn has no tools, and gets only Forgekeeper's facts about the change,
never comments.

A conflict update clears once the conflict ends or the PR/MR closes. A merge update stays
until you acknowledge it, because the merge is the news. Updates for targets the session
drops clear right away. Setting `watch.lifecycle` to `false` stops all three kinds, and
retarget proposals too, since nothing notices merges then.

### Stacked PRs/MRs

A target **builds on** another of the session's targets when it targets that one's source
branch in the same project, on the same host. Forgekeeper links them only when exactly one
target matches, and keeps the link once the parent merges, because forges may retarget the
dependent PR/MR or delete the merged branch at that point. Sharing a session doesn't make
two PRs/MRs a stack.

When a parent merges, its update lists each dependent, and `lifecycleExecution.parentMerged`
sets what Forgekeeper works out about them:

| Mode        | What happens                                                                          |
| ----------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `"notify"`  | The default. The update names the dependents and the branch they target, and no more. |
| `"prepare"` | Forgekeeper works out the listed actions and proposes them in the update.             |

`actions` lists what `prepare` works out, so it needs at least one. `parentMerged`
supports `"retarget"`:

```json
{
  "lifecycleExecution": { "parentMerged": { "mode": "prepare", "actions": ["retarget"] } }
}
```

Forgekeeper proposes retargeting a dependent to the branch the parent merged into, and only
when it still targets the parent's source branch in the same project. It reads the
dependent from the forge first, so one the forge already retargeted gets no proposal, and
neither does one that targets something else, closed, or merged. A parent from a fork
gets no proposal, since its branch lives in another project. Only dependents the session
still targets count.

Forgekeeper never retargets anything itself, and never rebases. GitLab retargets up to
four dependent MRs when the merge deletes the source branch, so a proposal usually means
the branch was kept, which may be deliberate. Retarget the MR yourself, and rebase it if
the parent was squashed, since its commits stay on the dependent branch. Each event keeps
the policy it happened under, and the stricter of that and the current policy applies, so
enabling `prepare` never reads dependents again for earlier merges.

`lifecycleExecution` has no policy for conflicts or failed jobs. To investigate failed jobs,
add a [`job-failed` rule](#investigate-failed-jobs) to `automation.rules` instead. An
invalid or unsupported policy, such as `"prepare"` without actions, falls back to
`"notify"`, and Forgekeeper shows an error toast saying which options it ignored.

## Prepare fixes from review feedback

Automation is off by default. To authorize selected reviewers for specific projects, add
rules to `automation.rules` in Forgekeeper's plugin options:

```json
{
  "automation": {
    "rules": [
      {
        "on": "review",
        "host": "gitlab.com",
        "projects": ["gitlab-org/gitlab"],
        "reviewers": ["GitLabDuo"],
        "action": "prepare"
      }
    ]
  }
}
```

Each rule names its trigger in `on`: `"review"` for review feedback, or `"job-failed"` to
[investigate failed jobs](#investigate-failed-jobs). Forgekeeper ignores a rule without one,
with an error toast.

Hosts, projects, and reviewer usernames must be exact, without wildcards. Forgekeeper resolves
usernames through the authenticated forge API and checks account IDs on the findings it reads.
Adding an account to `reviewBots` enables monitoring only; it does not authorize code changes.
The corresponding review source must still be enabled under `watch`.

For each new settled batch on a project with a matching rule, Forgekeeper counts all
non-archived root sessions explicitly targetin

  `{}` in branch mode. `targets` lists every target as `{ url, issueUrl? }`. `url` and

## Migrating from opencode-forge-session-title

Replace `opencode-forge-session-title` with `opencode-forgekeeper` in `opencode.json`. Upgrading
from `opencode-forgekeeper` 1.x works the same way, because 1.x used the same IDs as
`opencode-forge-session-title`.

| Entry point | Plugin ID                   | Stored state                                                                             |
| ----------- | --------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Server      | `opencode-forgekeeper`      | Session targets, owned title prefixes, human-review baselines, and pending notifications |
| CLI         | `pedropombeiro.forgekeeper` | None                                                                                     |

OpenCode scopes plugin storage by plugin ID, so nothing stored under the former ID,
`opencode-forge-session-title`, carries over:

- Sessions start in branch-based naming. Ask the agent to set their targets again.
- A title that kept a single-reference prefix from before, such as `[!456] Review`, now looks
  like a reference that you wrote. Until you set a target, the status follows that PR/MR, labeled
  "from the session title". Setting a target adds a second prefix, such as
  `[#12, !45] [!456] Review`. Remove the older prefix by hand. Older prefixes with two
  references, such as `[#12, !45]`, are replaced automatically.
- The first look at each PR/MR records a new review baseline, so comments posted before then
  aren't announced.
- Callers of the RPC need the new ID, `opencode-forgekeeper`.

With default options, a new checkout shows the footer. Enable the inbox to collect updates,
then set `delivery.reviews` to `summary` if you want automatic summaries. Set `status` to
`false` to keep only titles.

If you set options for `opencode-forgekeeper` 2.x, also see
[Upgrade from forgekeeper 2.x](#upgrade-from-forgekeeper-2x).

## Code layout

- `src/index.ts` wires the server: the forge catalogs from the options, with a shared
  concurrency limit for status, and title lookups.
- `src/server.ts` registers the tool, the server commands, the agent guidance, title
  reconciliation, and the RPC. `src/commands.ts` parses the commands' arguments and writes
  their reports.
- `src/status-server.ts` connects the status service to sessions, storage, notifications,
  and RPC events. `src/status-service.ts` holds the leases and decides which keys poll.
- `src/target.ts` parses, normalizes, changes, and formats session targets, and matches
  forge URLs against them.
- `src/limit.ts` bounds how many forge requests run at once.
- `src/title.ts` extracts branch issue numbers and reconciles title prefixes.
- `src/options.ts` reads the plugin's status options.
- `src/lookups.ts` answers the title's forge questions: the branch's newest PR/MR number
  and a PR/MR's source branch.
- `src/status-client.ts` holds the CLI's leases, snapshots, and per-directory settings.
  `src/client-core.ts` connects it to the RPC for both clients. `src/tui.tsx` renders the
  terminal footer, dialog, commands, and notices; `src/gui.tsx` renders the desktop pill,
  panels, commands, and notices.
  `src/notice.ts` decides which notices a CLI shows and which tabs it reopens.
- `src/forge.ts` defines the forge-neutral types, the `Forge` adapter interface, and
  `ForgeTraits` with its optional `automatedReview`, `feedback`, and `lifecycle`
  capabilities.
- `src/adapters/gitlab/feedback.ts` and `src/adapters/github/feedback.ts` read each forge's
  comments for its `feedback` capability.
- `src/adapters/gitlab/adapter.ts` and `src/adapters/github/adapter.ts` provide each forge's
  adapter and traits. Adapters own API calls, pagination, error classification, and status
  normalization. Traits cover
  everything else: hosts, URL parsing, reference syntax, vocabulary, and forge-specific
  footer and dialog content.
- `src/forges.ts` registers each forge's traits, classifies hosts, opens adapters, and
  parses URLs.
- `src/git.ts` resolves a checkout's remotes, branch, and pushed branch name.
- `src/locate.ts` picks each key's PRs/MRs. `src/store.ts` caches lookups, polls, backs off
  after failures, and discards lookups that started before a change. `src/format.ts`
  renders the footer and dialog.
- `src/automated-review-watch.ts` and `src/human-review-watch.ts` decide when to notify the
  agent. `src/review-request-watch.ts` finds new requests for your review and selects the
  author's replies for context. `src/adapters/gitlab/review-requests.ts` reads them from
  GitLab's activity notes.
- `src/review-monitoring.ts` configures the review watchers, stores their state, and records
  review updates in the inbox.
- `src/lifecycle-watch.ts` finds conflicts, failed jobs, merges, and stack links between lookups, and
  keeps each event until it reaches the inbox. `src/lifecycle-execution.ts` proposes retargets
  of stacked PRs/MRs.
- `src/lifecycle-notifications.ts` formats lifecycle updates, checks retarget proposals, and
  connects lifecycle events to the inbox. `src/feedback-cleanup.ts` identifies resolved,
  closed, and settled updates for removal.
- `src/adapters/gitlab/linked-notes.ts` finds and reads the notes review comments link to.
- `src/summary-delivery.ts` stores and delivers summary turns, restricts their model requests,
  and handles linked-note access. `src/review-summary.ts` formats their content.
- `src/review-automation.ts` selects batches for automation rules and runs each attempt.
  `src/review-automation-host.ts` connects it to sessions and forges, and
  `src/review-claim.ts` stores attempts, execution claims, checkout locks, and the worktrees
  Forgekeeper created in SQLite. `src/review-worktree.ts` finds, creates, checks, and removes
  the worktrees that linked sessions run in.
  `src/review-preparation.ts` and `src/job-investigation.ts` write the prompts and task
  instructions for preparing review fixes and investigating failed jobs.
- `src/keyed-queue.ts` serializes updates by session or record while allowing other keys to progress.

Shared code never compares a forge against a specific name. It asks the forge's traits, or
checks for a capability, instead. To add a forge, add its kind to `ForgeKind` and
`ReviewRequest`, implement `Forge` and `ForgeTraits`, and register the traits in
`src/forges.ts`.
